fact_check_verdict: PASS WITH CONDITIONS. Two adversarial validators plus a showrunner fetch. Read: the AGU release (November 24th) and its EurekAlert copy (not independent), the Crossref record and abstract of Krause et al., Earth's Future 10.1029/2026EF008820 (CC BY 4.0, online November 24th), Nature World News (November 25th, independent second source for the Alaska range), the Crossref record and abstract of the Krause and Rammig ESSOAr preprint 10.22541/essoar.15010630/v1 (posted October 17th, not peer reviewed), the Alaska Division of Forestry 2024 wildfire handout historical table, akfireinfo.com, and Veraverbeke et al. 2017 (Nature Climate Change). The Wiley full text returned 403 every time, so nothing is claimed from the paper's body. Conditions: (1) every Alaska figure, the bolt baseline, the 2019 training year and 'nearly sevenfold' come from the AGU release only, so they carry PER AGU and the word PROJECTION, and the scenario is HIGH EMISSIONS; (2) the range is the result, never a single number, and never 'will'; (3) the study did not model fire, so fire is Alaska context from the Division of Forestry, never a projection of the paper; (4) the preprint tests ML lightning models in general against LIS/OTD satellite data and does not name the Earth's Future model, so the film never says it tested or refuted this paper; (5) the convection and ice-crystal explanation is the release's narration, not a Krause quote; (6) the 11 percent is a model reconstruction, not a measured trend; (7) no contiguous US or Germany figures exist, none drawn; (8) Krause is never gendered, use the surname.

claims.spoken: A new study in the journal Earth's Future came out November 24th.
claims.verbatim_source: Crossref record, labelled non-quotation: published online 24 November 2026, Earth's Future vol. 14 no. 11, e2026EF008820
requires: ordinal date, no year on screen

claims.spoken: Researchers led by Andreas Krause at the Technical University of Munich.
claims.on_screen: ANDREAS KRAUSE · TECHNICAL UNIVERSITY OF MUNICH
claims.verbatim_source: "Andreas Krause, an Earth system scientist at the Technical University of Munich and the study's lead author"
requires: never gender Krause, use the surname

claims.spoken: The team trained a machine learning model on lightning and weather observations from one year, 2019.
claims.verbatim_source: "the team trained a machine learning model with lightning and climate observations from 2019"

claims.spoken: It's a type of model called X G Boost.
claims.verbatim_source: "using an XGBoost machine learning model"

claims.spoken: It learned from six everyday weather readings, temperature, rain, humidity, air pressure, wind and sunlight.
claims.on_screen: TEMPERATURE · RAIN · HUMIDITY · PRESSURE · WIND · SUN
claims.verbatim_source: "that included temperature, rainfall, humidity, air pressure, wind speed, and incoming radiation from the sun."
requires: six inputs, the abstract confirms six daily surface variables

claims.spoken: It learned where ground-striking lightning lands, at half-degree squares of the map.
claims.verbatim_source: "to predict CG lightning density over land at 0.5° resolution"

claims.spoken: Run on today's climate, most of Alaska got less than one ground strike per square kilometer a year.
claims.on_screen: MOST OF ALASKA · UNDER 1 STRIKE PER SQ KM A YEAR · 1995 TO 2014 · PER AGU
claims.verbatim_source: "when most of the state's total ground area received, on average, less than one bolt per square kilometer per year."
requires: most of the state, not all

claims.spoken: Under a high-emissions future, Alaska could get 116 to 594 percent more ground-striking lightning by the end of the century.
claims.verbatim_source: "Alaska, for instance, could get 116% to 594% more ground-striking lightning than during the baseline period"
requires: the whole range, never one end alone

claims.spoken: At the top of the range, that's nearly seven times today's lightning.
claims.verbatim_source: "upper estimates reaching nearly sevenfold the current lightning frequency by 2100"
requires: upper estimate, never the central estimate

claims.spoken: Across the world's land, the projection is 76 to 140 percent more ground strikes than in 1995 to 2014.
claims.verbatim_source: "reveal large increases of 76%–140% under a high-emission scenario (SSP3-7.0)"

claims.spoken: Run backward on the climate of the 1900s, the model estimates lightning rose about 11 percent over the century.
claims.verbatim_source: "the frequency of cloud-to-ground lightning rose 11% over the 20th century"
requires: model estimate, never a measured trend

claims.spoken: That's about 12 percent for every degree Celsius of warming.
claims.verbatim_source: "equivalent to about 12% for every degree Celsius of warming"

claims.spoken: In the future runs it gets nearly three times as sensitive, about 30 percent more lightning per degree.
claims.on_screen: RUN FORWARD · NEARLY 3X ITS OWN 12 · ABOUT 30% PER °C · COULD
claims.verbatim_source: "that relationship could become nearly three times as sensitive, bumping up lightning frequency by 30% for each degree of warming."

claims.spoken: Earlier studies projected about 8 to 17 percent per degree, and the release says the gap comes mostly from different math.
claims.verbatim_source: "project cloud-to-ground lightning frequency rising between 8% and 17% per degree of warming"
requires: the discrepancy stems mostly from different mathematical approaches, per AGU release

claims.spoken: Krause said, I was quite surprised that the projections were so high.
claims.on_screen: "I WAS QUITE SURPRISED THAT THE PROJECTIONS WERE SO HIGH." · ANDREAS KRAUSE · PER AGU
claims.verbatim_source: "I was quite surprised that the projections were so high," Krause said.

claims.spoken: Krause also said there is actually quite a large uncertainty about how lightning will respond to climate change.
claims.on_screen: "QUITE A LARGE UNCERTAINTY" · ANDREAS KRAUSE · PER AGU
claims.verbatim_source: "There is actually quite a large uncertainty about how lightning will respond to climate change,"
requires: a quoted fragment must survive being read alone

claims.spoken: Warmer air stirs up more convection in the clouds, but it could also mean fewer ice crystals high up.
claims.on_screen: MORE CONVECTION · FEWER ICE CRYSTALS? · PER AGU
claims.verbatim_source: "As climate change raises air temperatures around the globe, more convection stirs up the clouds" and "But warmer air could also mean fewer ice crystals high up in the atmosphere"
requires: release narration, never in Krause's mouth

claims.spoken: The researchers say the Amazon is the least certain, because its future climate may look vastly different from what the model trained on.
claims.on_screen: LEAST CERTAIN · FAR FROM THE TRAINING DATA · PER AGU
claims.verbatim_source: "projections for the Amazon carry the most uncertainty since future climate conditions there may look vastly different"
requires: about the Amazon, never said of Alaska

claims.spoken: A month earlier, Krause and co-author Anja Rammig posted a preprint arguing that lightning model test scores can overstate how well they project.
claims.verbatim_source: "common lightning-model evaluations can overstate projection skill"
requires: about lightning models in general, never says it tested this paper's model
Rammig is a co-author on both, per Crossref

claims.spoken: In that preprint, a simple benchmark that just predicts the average from the training data beat the machine learning models it tested.
claims.on_screen: SIMPLE AVERAGE · BEAT THE ML MODELS · PREPRINT · ON SATELLITE DATA
claims.verbatim_source: "We introduce a simple benchmark predicting the training-data mean lightning density" and "outperforms machine-learning models and traditional parameterizations"
requires: on satellite lightning data (LIS/OTD), per the preprint
the ML models it tested, never 'this model'

claims.spoken: Their advice is to test models in conditions that differ from the ones they trained on.
claims.verbatim_source: "test models under conditions differing from the training distribution"

claims.spoken: The Earth's Future paper says its model beat a simpler regression and three existing lightning formulas.
claims.on_screen: BEAT A REGRESSION + 3 EXISTING FORMULAS · PER THE PAPER
claims.verbatim_source: "outperforms an alternative multiple linear regression model as well as three existing parameterizations"

claims.spoken: In Alaska, lightning fires burned at least 93 percent of the wildfire acres every year from 2015 to 2024.
claims.on_screen: LIGHTNING FIRES · 93% TO 100% OF ACRES BURNED · 2015 TO 2024 · AK DIV. OF FORESTRY
requires: context, never a projection of the study

claims.spoken: In 2022 that was about 3.1 million acres, 99 percent from lightning fires.
claims.verbatim_source: Labelled non-quotation, 2022 column: Fires 594, Acres 3,111,316, Natural Acres 3,099,465, % Acres Lightning 99%

claims.spoken: The study didn't look at fire or how forests would handle more lightning.
claims.verbatim_source: "the study didn't delve into how forests would handle a rise in lightning."
requires: Nature World News also: this study did not model fire directly

claims.spoken: One stormy Sunday in June 2024 put nearly 7,000 strikes on Alaska.
claims.on_screen: ONE DAY · NEARLY 7,000 STRIKES · AK DIV. OF FORESTRY
claims.verbatim_source: "Thunderstorms on Sunday produced nearly 7,000 lighting strikes statewide, with a heavy concentration in Southwest Alaska."

claims.spoken: Co-author Sander Veraverbeke's earlier work found lightning ignitions in North America's boreal forests had increased since 1975.
claims.on_screen: LIGHTNING IGNITIONS UP SINCE 1975 · VERAVERBEKE ET AL. 2017
claims.verbatim_source: "We find that lightning ignitions have increased since 1975"
requires: boreal North America (Alaska and Northwest Territories)

reserve.fact: Bieniek et al. 2020: two downscaled projections estimate a doubling of interior Alaska lightning
reserve.reason: a second projection would muddy the range; hold

reserve.fact: Chen et al. 2021: Arctic permafrost summer lightning +112 +- 38% by 2081 to 2100 under RCP8.5
Krause: 'Trees basically evolved to adapt to the local lightning frequency.'
reserve.reason: forest framing the study did not model

cut.fact: 97.5% of Alaska area burned by lightning 2004 to 2023
Nature World News quote 'The next step is for other research groups...'
cut.reason: unattributed, not in the AGU release

cut.fact: Krause explaining convection vs ice crystals
the preprint tested the Earth's Future model
